nameStory: The name 'wormwood' comes from the plant's historical use as a remedy for intestinal worms, while 'absinthe' refers to its famous role as the key flavoring ingredient in the legendary green liqueur. The word 'absinthe' itself comes from the Greek 'apsinthion,' meaning 'undrinkable' - a reference to the plant's intensely bitter taste that made it perfect for medicinal tonics.
description: Absinthe wormwood is a silvery-gray, aromatic perennial herb that grows 2-4 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. The entire plant has a distinctive sage-like appearance with deeply divided, feathery leaves that give it a delicate, lacy texture. It produces tiny yellowish flower heads in dense clusters during late summer, though the flowers are quite inconspicuous compared to the striking foliage. This European native has naturalized in parts of New England, where it's sometimes grown as an ornamental or herb garden plant.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, fern-like leaves covered in silky white hairs that give them a silvery-gray appearance. Crush a leaf and you'll smell an intense, bitter, sage-like aroma that's unmistakably medicinal.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, bushy clumps 2-4 feet tall with multiple woody stems at the base. The whole plant has a distinctly silvery appearance from a distance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous yellowish flower heads arranged in dense, branching clusters. Individual flowers lack the showy petals typical of most daisy family members.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel soft and velvety due to dense, silky hairs. The foliage has a dusty appearance and feels almost woolly to the touch.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Woody at the base becoming herbaceous higher up, with a whitish or pale gray color that matches the foliage tone.

habitat: In New England, absinthe wormwood is most commonly found in cultivated settings like herb gardens, around old homesteads, or as an ornamental in perennial borders. When naturalized, it prefers well-drained, sunny locations such as roadsides, waste areas, and disturbed ground. It tolerates poor, rocky soils and drought conditions once established.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as silvery-gray shoots from the woody base, with the characteristic feathery leaves quickly developing their distinctive aroma and texture.
seasonality.summer: Foliage reaches full development with maximum silver coloration and aromatic intensity. Late summer brings the small, clustered flower heads.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads, and leaves may become more grayish as cooler weather arrives. The plant remains semi-evergreen in milder areas.
seasonality.winter: In New England, the herbaceous portions die back to woody stems near the ground, though some basal foliage may persist in protected locations.

funFact: This is the infamous plant that gave absinthe liqueur its reputation for causing hallucinations and madness in 19th-century Europe - though modern science has shown that the 'absinthe madness' was likely due to the extremely high alcohol content and toxic additives, not the wormwood itself!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other silvery artemisias like dusty miller or beach wormwood, but absinthe wormwood's leaves are more finely divided and have a much stronger, more medicinal smell. Memory trick: if it smells strong enough to be medicine, it's probably absinthe wormwood.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its notorious reputation, absinthe wormwood contains compounds that are only mildly toxic in normal quantities, and the liqueur absinthe has been legal again in most countries since the early 2000s. The plant has been used medicinally for thousands of years across many cultures.
compareHints: Absinthe wormwood is much more silvery and aromatic than common mugwort, which has green leaves with white undersides. Unlike the annual sweet annie, absinthe wormwood is perennial with woody stems at the base. Its leaves are more finely divided than most other regional artemisias, giving it an almost fern-like appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Artemisia species, common mugwort is the tallest and most common, with the most deeply divided leaves.
Unlike common mugwort which has green leaves with white undersides, hoary mugwort is silvery-white all over and much more compact.
Among New England's Artemisia species, field sagewort stands out for its preference for the driest, sandiest soils and its exceptionally finely-divided silvery leaves.

Silver wormwood stands out from its New England Artemisia relatives by its intensely silvery-white appearance - common mugwort has green tops to its leaves, while hoary mugwort is more coastal and has different leaf shapes.
Among New England's wormwoods, Sweet Annie is unique for its sweet fragrance and annual growth habit - most other wormwoods are perennial and smell bitter.
Among New England's Artemisia species, biennial wormwood has the most finely divided leaves - much more delicate-looking than the broader-lobed common mugwort or the silvery hoary mugwort.
